content_items.title: SpecifyaaS: Managing Ephemeral Repositories in Collections-Based Research

programme.title: SpecifyaaS: Managing Ephemeral Repositories in Collections-Based Research
programme.session: SYM20 Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
programme.abstract:
Specify 7 has substantially expanded the capacity of institutions to standardize efficient biodiversity data capture, management, and exchange during collections-based research. At the Swedish Museum of Natural History (NRM), data are maintained across multiple Specify instances, which includes databases for research programmes and projects. They support collaborative initiatives characterized by operational constraints that often differ greatly from those of the public repositories where research specimens will ultimately be deposited.

Here I describe the use of Specify 7 instances as “ephemeral repositories” within the biodiversity data network at the NRM. Although they are often broader in scope with respect to the data compiled, and less likely to persist as independent data aggregations, ephemeral repositories are critical staging arenas for data standardization, mobilization, and exchange. As an low-investment outcome from using Specify 7, that reduces reliance on bespoke or isolated data management solutions, Specify-as-a-Service is intended to support efficient transfer of information to downstream systems after phases of active research.

Investment in early standardization improves data quality and reduces duplication of effort during rounds of data capture. Extending IT infrastructure into the broader suite of institutional tools supporting collections-based research promotes the implementation of FAIR practices and consistent workflows. Providing SpecifyaaS to staff and research collaborators will strengthen data integration across research and collections systems, and increase the long-term data usability and applicability across a wider range of use cases.

content_items.summary: Kevin Holston explained how the Swedish Museum of Natural History runs its own local Specify 7 instances ('Specify as a Service') as ephemeral or semi-persistent repositories for researchers, rather than pushing them straight into the institutional collection database. He distinguished research-group collections of loaned, persistent vouchers from institutional programmes such as biobanks and the environmental specimen bank, whose semi-persistent vouchers are used up over time. As an example, he showed how a researcher's 16 years of Madagascar aquatic insect inventory became a Specify research database with 808 collecting events, organised event images and field sheets. He argued that these instances bring standards in early and act as laboratories of innovation for Specify.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Giving researchers their own lightweight Specify instances early in the research process standardises data from the start and eases later exchange with the institutional collection.
content_items.why_it_matters: Much specimen data is created in project spreadsheets before it ever reaches a collection database. Giving researchers compatible, low-commitment instances is a practical way to get standards and identifiers in early and to track derivatives and loaned material as their own objects.
key_points: NRM runs local Specify installations on its own infrastructure and spins up temporary instances, for example for visiting researchers, that are compatible with the institutional database.
Category 1 (research group/project): material is mostly on loan, vouchers are persistent, and the project repository has little motivation to record where things physically are.

Category 2 (research institution/programme, e.g. biobank, eDNA and environmental specimen bank): vouchers are semi-persistent and subject to depletion, and the repository must reflect the physical collection.
Historically, derivatives have been documented as voucher attributes rather than as independent objects, which limits tracking of objects, attributes and locations over time.

A researcher's Madagascar aquatic insect inventory became a Specify research database with 808 collecting events over 16 years of trips. An unexpected benefit was standardisation and the organisation of event images and field data sheets.
Holston repurposed the Specify storage tree to record provenance, i.e. loans, in his own research database, showing Specify's flexibility.
Instances can be 'furnished' (pre-loaded with collection data, like a furnished house or hotel) to give visitors a head start in digitising.

content_items.title: Applying Data Standards at the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh

programme.title: Applying Data Standards at the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh
programme.session: SYM20 Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
programme.abstract:
Data standards play a crucial role in enabling the dissemination, interoperability, and reuse of biodiversity knowledge. At the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh (RBGE), efforts over more than four decades have focused on aligning herbarium collection data with a wide range of cultural, historical, technological, and biodiversity data standards. This ongoing work reflects both the evolving nature of standards and the need to integrate legacy data with emerging frameworks.

Since the transition to the Specify Collections Management System (CMS) in 2022, RBGE has further refined its use of data standards to enhance data quality, interoperability, and connectivity. These developments support improved sharing and linking of RBGE’s herbarium data with collections and research initiatives worldwide, contributing to a more integrated global biodiversity knowledge infrastructure.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by name and institution. ASR renders MycoBank as 'MicroBank', CETAF as 'CTAF', DiSSCo as 'Disco', Roger Hyam as 'Roger Higham' and data lake as 'data lock'. No questions were asked.

content_items.summary: Robyn Drinkwater described how RBGE, a herbarium of about three million specimens with databasing since the mid-1970s, uses identifiers in Specify to standardise and link its data. She covered merging duplicate agents (up to four or five versions of a person from the legacy system) with Specify's agent merge tool and storing agent identifiers. She also covered IPNI, MycoBank and World Flora Online taxon identifiers, CETAF stable specimen URIs used since 2012, and forthcoming DiSSCo DOIs. The second half showed how identifiers link the herbarium with RBGE's three other collection systems (IrisBG, Koha, AtoM), with examples of watercolours linked to moss specimens and living plants linked to herbarium vouchers.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Identifiers are how RBGE is standardising legacy herbarium data and reconnecting items spread across four separate collection management systems.
content_items.why_it_matters: The talk shows why identifiers need to be structured and resolvable, not just stored. It also shows the practical steps (agent disambiguation, field restructuring, cross-system links) that an institution needs to publish linked, citable data.
key_points: RBGE has about three million specimens covering all traditionally 'plant' groups including diatoms, algae and oomycetes; about 1.5 million database records have passed through at least four database systems.
The legacy system had no unified agents table, which left four or five versions of some people. The Specify agent merging tool is helping to disambiguate them.
Specify's dedicated agent identifier field allows several identifiers per agent. Link-outs to ORCID and Wikidata are planned to help staff.

Taxon identifiers: IPNI IDs for vascular plants and MycoBank IDs for fungi, with World Flora Online IDs being tested. Both have been stored in the LSID field, and that mixed content prevents link-outs, so restructuring is needed.
CETAF stable identifiers have been used since 2012. They make specimens citable, and staff can link from the barcode field to images in the herbarium catalogue without importing images into Specify.

RBGE runs four systems: Specify (herbarium), IrisBG (living collection), Koha (library and artworks) and AtoM (archives). Identifiers are used to link, e.g., Greville moss watercolours in Koha to specimens, and living accessions to herbarium vouchers.
Next steps: GenBank/BOLD identifiers for DNA extractions, links to sequencing data, getting identifiers into the Darwin Core export, and a possible Scottish data lake.

content_items.title: From Legacy Data to FAIR Workflows: Standardising Biodiversity Collections Using Specify

programme.title: From Legacy Data to FAIR Workflows: Standardising Biodiversity Collections Using Specify
programme.session: SYM20 Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
programme.abstract:
The KwaZulu-Natal Museum manages eleven natural history collections supporting biodiversity research, education, and long-term preservation of African heritage. Like many institutions, historical collection data were distributed across spreadsheets, paper records, and inconsistent legacy systems, creating challenges for data quality, interoperability, specimen tracking, and data mobilisation.

To address these challenges, the museum implemented Specify as its primary collections management system. This enabled the development of standardised workflows for specimen cataloguing, accessioning, georeferencing, taxonomic management, loan tracking, image attachment, and data cleaning across eleven collections.

A major focus of implementation has been aligning institutional workflows with biodiversity informatics standards, FAIR data principles, and machine-readable data practices. Centralised data management has improved metadata consistency, reduced duplication, and strengthened quality control. Specify’s querying and export functions have also improved readiness for data sharing and publication to global biodiversity infrastructures such as Global Biodiversity Information Facility.

The museum has observed improved efficiency in data capture, transaction management, researcher support, and standardised staff training. This presentation highlights practical lessons from implementing standardised, interoperability-focused workflows within a South African museum context and demonstrates how legacy collection data can be transformed into FAIR, mobilisation-ready biodiversity datasets.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by chair as Siyabonga Zamisa from KwaZulu-Natal Museum. ASR renders NSCF as 'an SCF' and Darwin Core as 'down-core'.

content_items.summary: Siyabonga Zamisa described how the KwaZulu-Natal Museum moved its 11 natural history collections (over 430,000 records) from Access, Excel, catalogue cards and other systems into Specify by 2019. With support from the Natural Science Collections Facility, it then developed shared workflows. He walked through a Darwin Core-based template spreadsheet used by all collections, quality checks in OpenRefine before WorkBench upload, routine specimen-versus-database QA, and a publishing pipeline through the IPT to GBIF. Before this the museum had no collections in GBIF; seven of eleven are now published.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Standardised workflows, not just a new database, turned 11 differently managed collections into GBIF-ready data.
content_items.why_it_matters: This is a concrete African museum example of procedure and standards, not technology alone, driving data mobilisation, with measurable gains in publishing, cataloguing speed and loan processing.
key_points: 11 collections with over 430,000 records, the largest being Mollusca and Insecta. Previous systems included Access, Excel and Rapid, and all collections have been in Specify since 2019.
The problem was inconsistent practice: each collection had its own habits for capturing, tracking and sharing data, which slowed loans and data sharing.
A single template spreadsheet based on Darwin Core terms, with field explanations, is used across all 11 collections to ease WorkBench mapping.
Workflow: capture in template → data technician QC in OpenRefine → Specify WorkBench mapping and validation → upload.
Daily QA: randomly selected specimens are checked against their Specify records and both are corrected.
Publishing: Specify query export → OpenRefine QC → removal of sensitive species → IPT metadata and Darwin Core mapping → GBIF.
Results: from no collections in GBIF to seven of eleven, faster cataloguing and much shorter loan processing.

Digitisation alone was not enough; putting information into a database does not automatically create good data management.
Before Specify and the workflows the museum had no collections in GBIF; now seven of eleven are published.

recommendations: Standardise the workflow around specimens, data, people and standards, not just the database.
results_findings: Seven of 11 collections now published to GBIF (none before).
Significantly reduced loan processing and turnaround time.

q_and_a.answer_summary: Curators were asked how they wanted their forms; roughly 20% is customised per collection and the rest is common across all 11. Staff use Specify at different levels, with the data technician overseeing.

content_items.title: Digitize, Standardize, Mobilize: Wildlife Biodiversity Biobanking with Specify

programme.title: Digitize, Standardize, Mobilize: Wildlife Biodiversity Biobanking with Specify
programme.session: SYM20 Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
programme.abstract: Biodiversity biobanks are increasingly recognized as critical research infrastructures supporting conservation, genomics, species management, and One Health initiatives through the long-term preservation of samples and associated metadata. While the physical preservation and curation of samples remains central to biobanking, the scientific value of these collections depends on the generation of high-quality, standardized, and interoperable data. As biodiversity research advances toward implementation of FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles and the Extended Specimen concept, these biobanks face challenges in managing multidimensional datasets that extend beyond individual samples to include taxonomic, spatial, genetic, regulatory, and derivative information. Within the SANBI Wildlife Biobank, collections include diverse taxa and sample types such as blood, tissues, DNA extracts, and cell cultures linked to permits, storage records, images, molecular data, and metadata. Historically, these data were distributed across disconnected spreadsheets, paper records, folders, and external drives, creating challenges in data consistency, accessibility, and long-term sustainability. The implementation of Specify has transformed collection workflows from fragmented data management practices into an integrated relational framework capable of linking specimens, tissue collections, storage information, compliance documentation, and taxonomic data within a single system. The use of hierarchical taxonomy structures, controlled vocabularies, unique identifiers, and customizable workflows has improved data consistency, sample traceability, quality control processes, and transformed biodiversity biobanks from static repositories into dynamic digital resources.

actual.identification_notes: Speaker introduced herself as manager of the SANBI Wildlife Biobank. ASR renders SAIAB as 'SAIB' and SANBI as 'Sanbi'. The Q&A question came from Kevin Holston (addressed as 'Kevin').

content_items.summary: Kim Labuschagne presented the SANBI Wildlife Biobank, which holds samples and e-vouchers rather than whole specimens. It has over 250,000 samples from more than 110,000 animals in 46 countries, covering about 1,900 species including many threatened ones. She explained why an extended-specimen data model is needed to link samples, derivatives, permits, storage history, molecular data and publications, and how implementing Specify around 2013 replaced disconnected spreadsheets and records. Key features are the taxon, storage (bank→freezer→rack→box→position) and geography trees, attachments for permits and chain-of-custody photos, and customisable workflows.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Specify's hierarchical trees and attachments turned a fragmented wildlife biobank into a traceable extended-specimen data system.
content_items.why_it_matters: Biobanks are growing conservation and genomics infrastructure, and their value depends on tracing every aliquot, permit and derived dataset back to the individual animal.
key_points: The biobank was established in 1994 and holds over 250,000 samples from more than 110,000 individual animals from 46 countries, spanning 14 phyla and nearly 1,900 species.
Many holdings are threatened on the IUCN Red List, including the extinct western black rhino.
79 different sample types are stored from room temperature down to -196 °C. Every freezer-to-freezer move is a QC point that must be recorded.

The data model has moved from 'tissue sample + catalogue number' to an extended specimen with voucher, field metadata, permits, storage history, DNA extraction, genome sequence, disease screening and publications.
Specify was implemented around 2013, with support from SAIAB, to replace disconnected systems.
The storage tree locates samples down to position in a box. Catalogue numbers plus barcodes prevent searching through hundreds of boxes.
Attachments hold permits (including CITES and disease regulations), data sheets and chain-of-custody photographs.

content_items.title: Integrating Specify in broader Science infrastructure

programme.title: Integrating Specify in broader Science infrastructure
programme.session: SYM20 Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
programme.abstract:
At the Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria, Specify is used to deliver high-quality data to the Australasian Virtual Herbarium (AVH), as well as managing the herbarium's holdings and transactions like loan and exchange. Specify is embedded in our broader science infrastructure and we have built various extensions and integrations.

We make use of the flexibility of Specify to handle complex workflows. We use a separate discipline, rather than the Borrows table, to manage loans from other institutions. This way we can link up images and DNA sequences we have taken to specimens data, while keeping the data separate from the National Herbarium of Victoria (MEL) collection. We also use "staging" collections for exchange data, so we can make sure we have the specimens and validate the data before it is incorporated into the main collection. There is also a dedicated collection for the Victorian Conservation Seed Bank, which shares most of its data with the main collection.

We have a "bystander" application that provides functionality that Specify does not have or where the Specify functionality does not quite fit our workflows, e.g., handling ZPL-based label-printing, storage assignment and loan returns.

The Specify taxon tree functions as the taxonomic point of truth for our Digital Asset Management System (DAMS). At the same time, we have applications to sync the Specify taxon tree with national and global taxonomies, including VicFlora, APC, AusMoss, AusFungi, Plants of the World Online (PoWo), Bryonames and Tropicos.

The AVH is our collection's portal in to the world. We use the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) Integrated Publishing Toolkit (IPT) to publish collections data to AVH.

content_items.summary: Niels Klazenga described how RBG Victoria, a Specify user for over 16 years, embeds Specify as a 'collections hub' among other hubs: a Canto digital asset management system, VicFlora, a documentation hub, a traits hub of Lucid keys, KeyBase, and the Australasian Virtual Herbarium within the Atlas of Living Australia, which is its only dissemination channel. A separate 'bystander' application and a GraphQL API provide what Specify lacks or does differently, such as ZPL label printing, duplicate labels, partial loan returns, an event system and taxonomy syncing. He noted that moving from ABCD to Darwin Core felt like a step back and that a more structured model will help. He also called for Specify to support linking identifications to taxon concepts.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Specify works best at RBG Victoria as one component of a wider hub-based science infrastructure, with custom tools filling its gaps.
content_items.why_it_matters: Real-world integration patterns, such as a taxon tree as backbone for other systems, a GraphQL API feeding a IIIF image portal, and IPT-to-ALA-to-GBIF delivery, show how a CMS fits into institutional infrastructure and where CMS vendors could improve.
key_points: RBG Victoria started with Specify 6.0.1 and chose Specify mainly to deliver high-quality data to AVH.

Hubs: Specify (collections), Canto (media/DAMS), VicFlora (flora of Victoria and horticultural flora of south-eastern Australia), a documentation hub, a traits hub (Lucid keys) and KeyBase (pathway keys).
Specify is not used for dissemination; all data go through AVH/ALA via the IPT, and ALA passes them on to GBIF as Australia's GBIF node.

A bystander app handles things Specify cannot, e.g. starting label printing mid-sheet on sheets of 30, ZPL labels for new printers (PDF quality too low), duplicate labels, partial loan returns and an event system.
The Specify taxon tree is the taxonomic backbone for other applications such as the image portal and living collections database, synced via a GraphQL API that predates Specify's own API.
A IIIF-compliant image portal is under development; Specify data populates the IIIF Presentation API.
Seed bank germination tests and orchid conservation data do not fit Specify and will get separate databases.
Taxon concepts: many are recorded as taxon citations, but identifications need to link to taxon concepts.

content_items.title: The Good, the Bad, and the Standardised: A Specify Journey Through 200 Years of the MfN Berlin's Biological Collections

programme.title: The Good, the Bad, and the Standardised: A Specify Journey Through 200 Years of the MfN Berlin’s Biological Collections
programme.session: SYM20 Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
programme.abstract: The foundations of the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin (MfN)´s biological collections laid as early as 1810, houses today around 30 million specimens from the fields of palaeontology, zoology, botany and geology, as well as archives and modern media such as a sound library, reflecting 200 years of scientific, technical, colonial and political upheavals. Colonial collections (such as the Tendaguru excavation which returned 225 tons of dinosaur fossils), wars (the 1945 bombings destroyed a considerable number of specimens) and the Cold War isolation have left behind fragmented, multilingual and ethically complex data. Following reunification, resistance to digital transformation and the heterogeneity of legacy systems (paper labels, Excel, local databases), which persist to this day, hinder the standardisation of this complex yet essential biodiversity data. Today, we are in the process of transitioning to Specify as our sole collection management system (CMS): this powerful tool enables us to standardise metadata (Darwin Core), manage the MfN’s 22 collections, fill scientific gaps (missing labels, obsolete taxonomy) and manage permissions for over 100 users, with specific needs, whilst meeting modern requirements (GBIF exports, 3D scanning). We are also exploring ways to fill historical gaps by linking colonial archives to specimens (for example, the roles of workers at Tendaguru via Wikidata in the DTE project), using specific tables to reintegrate overlooked elements. This presentation will share the lessons learnt from 200 years of upheaval: how Specify helps to preserve biodiversity data and reconstruct history, as well as the work that remains to be done to meet all these needs.

actual.identification_notes: Chair and speaker name rendered as 'Marion Duprette' by ASR. ASR renders the Tendaguru expedition as 'Thünen-Gohr Expedition', Tanga as 'Tanga, Uro' and Franziska Böttger as 'Franziska Bottger'. The Soviet repatriation year is transcribed as 1943, which is presumably an ASR/speech error for the 1950s. The questioner identified as being from Agriculture Canada.

content_items.summary: Marion Depraetere traced how the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin's history shaped its data: colonial expeditions such as Tendaguru, the 1945 bombing, Soviet confiscation and return, Cold War isolation, pandemic-era reliance on personal Excel files, and an October 2023 cyberattack that ended debate and made Specify the sole CMS. All 30 collections are now in one Specify instance, which enables cross-collection reporting. Specify's flexibility supports decolonisation work through a one-to-many historical-events table and a prototype 'Historical Context' collection linking archive letters to specimens. She highlighted the gap between political geography (ISO 3166) and ecological or marine units, and argued that standardisation should respond to a need rather than be imposed.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Specify's flexibility lets MfN consolidate 30 historically complex collections into one database while starting to reconstruct colonial and wartime history, but geography and historical events remain unsolved.
content_items.why_it_matters: Many large museums face the same combination of legacy heterogeneity, colonial provenance and diverse audiences. The talk shows practical data-model workarounds and the open problem of representing administrative and ecological geography together.
key_points: MfN holds about 30 million items across 30 collections and sub-collections, managed by about 60 staff and support people.
History affects the data: colonial expeditions, the 1945 bombing (75% of the collection saved, losses still unclear), Soviet confiscation and repatriation, and Cold War isolation.
Specify was first adopted in 2010 (mammals first). The pandemic reinforced personal tools. The October 2023 cyberattack halted MfN for nearly a year and confirmed Specify as the sole CMS.

All 30 collections sit in a single Specify instance, allowing standardisation while keeping collection-specific features and giving single-query reports (e.g. entries per year, percentage of objects with IDs).
For decolonisation, a repurposed one-to-many table links objects to historical events, and a prototype 'Historical Context' collection links a 1909 letter from Tanga to the objects it mentions.

Political boundaries (ISO 3166) aid interoperability but do not match ecological, biogeographic or marine units. Options are extra locality fields (complex, error-prone) or a second geography tree based on GeoNames or Marine Regions, not yet tested.
Standardisation 'must remain a response to a need rather than a solution to a problem'.
methods: historical-events table linked to collection objects
prototype archive collection linking letters to specimens
questions: How can administrative and ecological/marine geographies be represented together without losing information?

programme.abstract:
The Specify Collections Consortium (SCC) supports research collections around the world with Specify Software, an intuitive, robust, and highly-customizable software platform for digitizing holdings and managing collections. For over 25 years, Specify has supported biological research collections, biorepositories, and now geological research collections, with its open-source software for managing and publishing collections data.

Ensuring your collections data meets Biodiversity Standards means it will be more accessible to the scientific community and research. Over the last year, the SCC has focused our efforts on enabling members to more easily meet biodiversity standards during data entry and making shared data more accessible and interoperable.

In this presentation, SCC staff will discuss the soon to be integrated Darwin Core standards in the data model, making publishing to data aggregators such as the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF), the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA), the Global Genome Biodiversity Network (GGBN), and Integrated Digitized Biocollections (iDigBio) easier while maintaining the customizability and flexibility upon which Specify was built.

The SCC is a collaborative collections community governed, funded, and sustained by its member institutions. Our software and technical support priorities address member and system infrastructure needs. Specify software enables natural history museums to curate, integrate, and publish data from a single, robustly-engineered platform for biological and geological collections.

Since 2022, the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) has migrated five of its collections into separate instances of Specify. This in turn allows for a more streamlined process for sharing data and the use of ETL tools to export the data into external aggregators such as the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA). It also facilitates the use of API-based integration to connect to extended specimen metadata repositories, increasing the reach and interoperability of our data.

content_items.title: A metadata-first FAIR4AI checklist and automated evaluation agent for biodiversity datasets

programme.title: A metadata-first FAIR4AI checklist and automated evaluation agent for biodiversity datasets
programme.session: SYM25A From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
As AI methods become increasingly integral to ecology and biodiversity science, the data that are used must meet standards beyond traditional FAIR principles. In a cross-community workshop with data providers, infrastructure operators, and AI/ML practitioners, we refined definitions for three tiers of data readiness: FAIR data meet established open-science norms; FAIR4AI criteria extend those norms with metadata sufficient for AI systems to discover, assess, and stage datasets to enable their use at scale without manual intervention; and AI-ready data have been fully prepared for specific AI-enabled applications. These distinctions are important because the gap between FAIR and FAIR4AI appears to be primarily a metadata gap, not a lack of technical infrastructure, and closing it is necessary to successfully use emerging AI tools in ecological synthesis.

To make these distinctions actionable, we developed a FAIR4AI checklist adapted from the Earth Science Information Partners (ESIP) AI-Readiness Checklist and the Imageomics Institute's Dataset Card and Metadata Checklists, with additions for biodiversity-specific concerns including taxonomic resolution, spatial and temporal extent, annotation provenance, and instrumentation metadata. Evaluation questions span Provenance, General Information, Data Structure, Data Origin, Data Processing, Data Quality, Guidance and Recommendations, and Data Access. We then built an open-source, LLM-powered evaluation tool to ingest a dataset’s metadata and return evidence-based responses to each evaluation question along with per-category FAIR scores.

Advancing FAIR4AI standards in biodiversity will require community input to ensure they support AI applications in ways that are consistent with community ethics and goals.

content_items.summary: Tanya Berger-Wolf presented the NSF-funded FAIR for AI Bio project (FAIROS programme), which has built AI-ready data infrastructure for ecology through a series of community workshops since August 2025. The project distinguishes FAIR, FAIR4AI (machine-findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable, so AI-ready datasets can be prepared with minimal human intervention) and AI-ready (application-specific) data, within a question–data–model round-tripping framework. The team built a checklist that grew from four categories (structural, scientific, provenance, governance) to 96 items, and an LLM agent that scores datasets, gives item-level recommendations and compares FAIR and FAIR4AI scores. content_items.title: Phenobase: a harmonized, AI-ready knowledge base of global plant phenology

programme.title: Phenobase: a harmonized, AI-ready knowledge base of global plant phenology
programme.session: SYM25A From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract: Plant phenology shapes ecosystem dynamics, species interactions and serves as a sensitive indicator of environmental change. Sources of global phenology data have exponentially increased but remain siloed and fragmented. In situ monitoring networks produce rigorous repeated observations, but are typically regional and disconnected. Digitized herbarium specimens and community-science platforms such as iNaturalist offer vast spatial, temporal, and taxonomic breadth but phenology information is latent in images and unstructured metadata. Phenobase addresses these gaps by assembling these sources into a harmonized knowledge base. We first applied computer-vision models (PhenoVision and PhenoVision-Leaf) to score presence of open flowers, fruits, breaking leaf buds, green leaves, and colored leaves across tens of millions of iNaturalist records. We used an different, ensemble-based ML model approach trained via expert annotations for labeled flowers on herbarium sheets to score millions of available imaged herbarium sheets. Finally, we assembled in-situ monitopring data from USA-NPN, NEON, PhenObs, Budburst, and SeasonWatch. Phenobase harmonizes these sources using the Plant Phenology Ontology which maps source-specific phenophase terms to shared trait concepts while preserving contextual metadata. Model certainty thresholds, validation accuracies, ML model version, and family-level performance metrics travel with each record, so downstream users can filter on quality. Phenobase data are openly available and show how machine-learning extraction, ontology-based integration, and standardized provenance metadata turn heterogeneous biodiversity collections into AI-ready data products. We close by discussing next-step challenges with maintaining and growing such resources.

content_items.title: From 1.5 Billion Raw Queries to AI-Ready Biodiversity Data: Human-AI Collaborative Curation Pipelines in Pl@ntNet

programme.title: From 1.5 Billion Raw Queries to AI-Ready Biodiversity Data: Human-AI Collaborative Curation Pipelines in Pl@ntNet
programme.session: SYM25A From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Large biodiversity platforms collect massive volumes of opportunistic observations that are valuable for ecological research and AI model training. However, transforming these heterogeneous user contributions into trustworthy and reusable biodiversity data remains a major challenge. Pl@ntNet currently processes more than 1.5 billion user queries consisting of plant images and associated metadata submitted by a large international community. Only a small fraction of these data ultimately become AI-ready training data (~25M images) or research-grade occurrences shared with GBIF (~2.5M images).

We present the human-AI collaborative curation pipeline used in Pl@ntNet to progressively transform raw multimodal observations into fitness-for-use biodiversity datasets. The pipeline combines automated filtering, community moderation, collaborative taxonomic revision, image-quality assessment, and governance constraints. Automated filters remove non-plant content, malformed observations, duplicate or low-quality images, and sensitive media. Taxonomic quality is refined through a collaborative validation process combining AI predictions, community interactions, and expert feedback across species galleries and observation streams. Community moderation signals help identify problematic observations, including off-topic or unreliable content. Dataset construction also incorporates licensing and provenance constraints, excluding observations that cannot be redistributed or reused.

We further show how downstream objectives require different curation levels. While AI training datasets prioritize taxonomic consistency, visual relevance, and diversity, GBIF publication requires stricter filters on geolocation, cultivation status, metadata completeness, and interoperability standards.

content_items.summary: Alexis Joly described the curation pipeline that turns Pl@ntNet's 1.6 billion raw, highly opportunistic image queries (from about 20 million users a year, including house plants, tattoos, people and sensitive content) into AI training data and GBIF occurrences. Every image passes a main model trained on about 25 million human-validated images, which includes 'reject' classes. He called that reject classifier the hardest part and an editorial choice. Opt-in public observations enter human curation with weighted majority voting, where each user's weight reflects expertise estimated by an EM algorithm. Other observations contribute only automatically filtered occurrences above a strict confidence threshold (<0.01% error) and a wildness classifier to GBIF. He warned about feedback loops in which users follow AI errors.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Pl@ntNet's human–AI pipeline filters a vast, noisy stream into two GBIF datasets and training data, with separate branches for opted-in human-validated and automatic occurrence-only data.
content_items.why_it_matters: Opportunistic AI apps are among the largest sources of biodiversity observations. How they filter, validate, licence and publish data determines the quality of downstream models and species distribution analyses.
key_points: Pl@ntNet is 15 years old, has about 20 million users a year, 1.6 billion raw observations and about 20,000 plants per hour.
The raw stream includes cultivated and potted plants, plants on clothing and tattoos, humans (e.g. classroom sessions), non-living objects, nudity and drug-related images.

The main model, trained on ~25 million human-validated images, outputs species, genus, family, diseases and reject classes. The reject classifier is the hardest and involves editorial choices about user intent.

Branch 1: observations users opt in to share publicly (CC BY-SA, named) are curated by weighted majority voting, with user expertise estimated by an EM algorithm based on the number of species a user can recognise.
Validated data retrain the model regularly, and old queries are reprocessed.
Branch 2: non-shared observations contribute only occurrences (no images) above a per-model threshold with <0.01% error; about 150 million remain after this filter.

A wildness classifier (trained on anthropised context and the app's cultivated tag) and WCVP level-2 country flora filtering remove cultivated plants before GBIF publication; two GBIF datasets result.
Feedback loops: when users follow AI errors, contamination can cause some species' identifications to drift over a decade.

content_items.title: From Sensor to Species: AI-Assisted Segmentation, Deep Learning Workflows, and Persistent Biodiversity Records from Earth Observation Systems

programme.title: From Sensor to Species: AI-Assisted Segmentation, Deep Learning Workflows, and Persistent Biodiversity Records from Earth Observation Systems
programme.session: SYM25A From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Advances in airborne and spaceborne Earth observation systems are enabling increasingly detailed ecological analyses across global spatial and temporal scales. RGB, multispectral, and hyperspectral imaging platforms (ie: Landsat, Sentinel-2, NASA AVIRIS-NG, EMIT, and the National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) Imaging Spectrometer) provide opportunities to identify vegetation structure, phenology, and potentially species-level ecological patterns from remotely sensed imagery . However, airborne and spaceborne remotely sensed biodiversity observations remain comparatively underrepresented within biodiversity informatics infrastructures such as the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF).

This presentation explores a biodiversity informatics workflow for transforming sensor-derived ecological observations into persistent, interoperable biodiversity records. The workflow integrates foundation-model segmentation approaches, including the Segment Anything Model (SAM), object-based image analysis [8], and DeepForest tree crown delineation workflows. These approaches are combined with AI-assisted species classification and Darwin Core standards to generate candidate biodiversity occurrence records from remotely sensed vegetation objects.

A central focus of the project is the introduction of persistent identifiers for segmented vegetation objects, enabling longitudinal monitoring of ecological entities across repeated temporal observations. The presentation will discuss interoperability challenges, provenance and uncertainty representation, and opportunities for integrating AI-generated ecological observations into biodiversity informatics infrastructures and biodiversity monitoring workflows.

content_items.title: On-Device AI for Data Cleaning, Standardisation, and Exploration in Collections Management

programme.title: On-Device AI for Data Cleaning, Standardisation, and Exploration in Collections Management
programme.session: SYM25A From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract: Museums operate across a diverse landscape of legacy data systems and formats, reflecting the long history of collections management and digitisation efforts. These include heterogeneous database structures, varied metadata standards, and unstructured or semi-structured records derived from historical catalogues and specimen labels. A key component of ongoing work is the standardisation and transformation of these legacy data into consistent, interoperable formats aligned with modern biodiversity data standards. This presentation focuses on the use of local/on-device AI systems to support the cleaning, standardisation and exploration of collections dataspread across legacy systems, including collections management records, storage location data, specimen locality information, geographic coordinates and bibliographic references. We demonstrate how AI can be applied to transform unstructured and semi-structured records into consistent, interoperable data aligned with modern biodiversity standards. Using dedicated hardware such as Dell GB10 systems and high-performance development devices, the platform provides AI-assisted suggestions for improving data quality, identifying inconsistencies and highlighting missing or ambiguous information across both collections management systems and exported datasets. It also enables interactive exploration, allowing users to query, interrogate and summarise collections data in real time.This allows the platform to generate summarised insights, identify patterns and relationships, and highlight areas requiring further curation or standardisation. A live demo will show how local AI systems can support large-scale data transformation and contribute to the development of standardised, high-quality and AI-ready collections data.

content_items.title: FAIR, CLEAR, and Causal: A semantic framework for ecological knowledge synthesis

programme.title: FAIR, CLEAR, and Causal: A semantic framework for ecological knowledge synthesis
programme.session: SYM25A From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Ecological synthesis produces knowledge that is human-interpretable but rarely machine-actionable. Attempts to address this through RDF/OWL-based semantic representations introduce a new problem: structures become opaque even to domain experts. We present the Semantic Units Framework, a modular approach to structuring ecological data and knowledge as logic-aware, independently addressable units aligned with the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) and CLEAR (Cognitively interoperable, semantically Linked, contextually Explorable, easily Accessible, human-Readable and -interpretable) Principles.

The central contribution is embedding causal knowledge within this architecture. Universal causal statement units encode causal hypotheses as addressable graph entities forming a navigable semantic grid, like a spatial map, to which evidence, publications, and contextual qualifiers can be anchored. Individual observations can be linked to causal hypotheses they support or contradict, enabling queries such as “Which data support this causal claim?” This supports semi-automated causal reasoning, confounder detection, and AI-ready evidence-gap maps.

The framework decomposes knowledge graphs into (a) statement units as single propositions with a persistent identifier, provenance, and method links and (b) compound units grouping related statement units into reusable knowledge objects, both serializable as nanopublication FAIR Digital Objects. Machine-interpretable structures are decoupled from human-facing representations via dynamic labels and graphs, keeping OWL/RDF accessible without specialist knowledge. Currently conceptual with partial prototypes, we invite discussion toward its community-driven realisation.

actual.identification_notes: Programme lists no speaker; the chair introduced 'Lars Vogt's presentation' and Vogt presented the EcoWeaver Semantic Units approach to causal knowledge, matching the abstract. Ten-minute slot; no questions due to lunch.

content_items.summary: Lars Vogt presented a purely conceptual framework, developed in the EcoWeaver initiative, for representing causal ecological knowledge with Semantic Units. Using Darwin's naturalisation conundrum (phylogenetic relatedness can raise or lower establishment success), he modelled causal relations as binary relations between change processes. He introduced universal causal statement units with their own identifiers, provenance and asserted/not-asserted status, so contradictory claims can coexist without logical inconsistency. Paths, networks and causal perspectives get addresses in a 'semantic grid', like map addresses. Evidence, cases (linked via a negatable 'satisfies' statement), conditions, measurement methods for unobservable variables and formal model readings can be pinned to them.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Semantic Units can turn ecological causal claims into addressable, versioned graph objects to which evidence and failures can be pinned, helping ecology accumulate rather than merely accrue causal knowledge.
content_items.why_it_matters: Ecological synthesis produces causal claims faster than they are consolidated. A representation that keeps contradictory claims, their evidence and their contexts queryable could support evidence-gap mapping and causal modelling.
key_points: Running example: Darwin's naturalisation conundrum, with pre-adaptation and limiting-similarity paths giving opposite effects from the same cause.
Causal relationships are modelled as binary relations between processes of change in qualities or dispositions and their bearers.

Three requirements: support intervention reasoning (AAA principle of actionable knowledge), distinguish general claims from particular cases, and represent change processes and methods for quantifying unobservable qualities.

Many needed statement types are not supported by OWL semantics, hence Semantic Units: one identifier per semantically meaningful unit, technology-agnostic, with dynamic labels/graphs for CLEAR human readability, and negation in the A-box without complex class axioms.
Universal causal statement units carry provenance, literature source and extraction method, and whether the proposition is asserted, so contradictory claims can coexist.
Compound units give identifiers to paths, networks and causal perspectives (including chains, forks and colliders), forming a semantic grid comparable to OpenStreetMap addresses.
Cases are linked to universal claims through a 'satisfies' statement that can be negated to record failures, making failures easy to query. All units are versioned and citable.

questions: How should families of causal hypotheses be split into applicability and failure spaces?

content_items.title: Mobilising and integrating extracted information from the literature into a biodiversity data ecosystem - the BIOfid approach

programme.title: Mobilising and integrating extracted information from the literature into a biodiversity data ecosystem - the BIOfid approach
programme.session: SYM25B From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Insufficient data availability is a critical bottleneck for biodiversity research. The fact that countless species are going extinct before they can even be collected and described is a particularly alarming aspect of our lack of knowledge and data. Another aspect is that vast quantities of data already exist but remain largely inaccessible-namely, data locked in unstructured, unindexed literature. These biodiversity data must be urgently mobilized to support research. The term 'mobilization' can take on different meanings. The most basic approach is to digitize printed publications and make them freely available online, allowing them to 'circulate globally' and allowing their content be discovered through keyword searches. However, since the vocabulary, organism names, and geographic terms used in publications vary considerably over time, normalization is essential to enable both efficient searches and integration with other data sources.

This normalization is achieved through annotation based on generic and domain-specific standards, with TDWG playing a central role in defining the latter. Two examples illustrate this: Only when species names are linked to a taxonomic backbone like GBIF’s, and when terms for morphological traits are connected to TraitBank, can researchers efficiently explore the wealth of data on a species’ characteristics hidden in literature-despite its heterogeneity in language, publication year, or writing style. Against this background, this presentation demonstrates how the Discipline-Specific Information Service Biodiversity Rersearch (BIOfid) addresses these challenges and how biodiversity data from the BIOfid corpus can be transformed into a graph-compatible format and made robot-ready for AI applications.

content_items.summary: Gerwin Kasperek argued that literature is the only biodiversity data source combining historical depth with high volume, but its data are locked in multilingual, abbreviation-heavy, sometimes poorly printed text. Using an 18th-century German passage about an orchid near Frankfurt, he showed the occurrence and trait records that could be extracted. He then showed a current LLM getting taxon and habitat right but hallucinating GBIF and Wikidata IDs, even after prompt improvements, so outputs must be verified against authoritative sources. He presented BIOfid, the DFG-funded specialised information service run by Senckenberg and Goethe University Frankfurt, with its annotated corpus, Unified Corpus Explorer, NLP pipelines, ontologies and plans for multimodal extraction into RDF/OWL knowledge graphs.

content_items.why_it_matters: Centuries of occurrence and trait data exist only in print. Standard-based, verifiable extraction pipelines are needed before such data can safely feed knowledge graphs and AI.
key_points: Collections data have depth but limited volume, and citizen science has volume but only recent years; literature combines both but is the hardest to access.
Challenges: natural language, non-English texts (German, Latin, Hungarian), insider abbreviations, domain conventions such as indented keys, poor print quality.

BIOfid aims: mobilise data from Central European literature, provide text-mining tools, digitise 20th-century literature; a collaboration of Senckenberg, Goethe University text technology and the Senckenberg Library, funded by DFG.

Uses the generic standards UIMA, OWL and RDF/SPARQL and the domain standards Darwin Core and GBIF/Catalogue of Life backbones. Reusable components are DUUI, the Unified Corpus Explorer (UCE) and ontologies (e.g. Chilopoda anatomy, EnvO extensions and translations).

content_items.title: Camtrap DP: extending data standard designed for camera trapping research to support AI workflows and new data sources

programme.title: Camtrap DP: extending data standard designed for camera trapping research to support AI workflows and new data sources
programme.session: SYM25B From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Passive sensor monitoring is generating multimodal biodiversity data at unprecedented scale. As AI becomes central to processing these datasets, standards must evolve to capture not only what was observed, but how, preserving the full provenance of human and machine annotations.

Camtrap DP is an open data exchange standard for camera trap data, developed under TDWG. Built on the Frictionless Data framework, it natively integrates AI-relevant data (bounding boxes, classification probabilities, method attribution and model name). With multiple datasets published via GBIF, it has demonstrated clear value for interoperable, research-ready wildlife monitoring data.

Expanding adoption has now exposed important gaps. The Safe and Sound bioacoustics project and the Insect AI community - both evaluating Camtrap DP as a candidate standard for their data - highlight shared needs alongside feedback from traditional camera trap users: including more expressive hardware description, flexible recording schedule specification, and richer support for AI-generated data.

While the framework's flexibility permits ad-hoc extensions, community-wide standardization is essential to ensure data remains FAIR and comparable across projects. We are therefore developing a new version of Camtrap DP that formalizes these needs through new standardized tables covering AI model provenance and the complete record of detections and annotations, rather than only final consensus results.

We present the community consultation process driving these developments and the proposed changes to the data model and controlled vocabularies, situating this work within the broader challenge of evolving domain-specific standards to meet a rapidly changing, AI-driven data landscape.

content_items.summary: Karolina Kuczkowska introduced Camtrap DP, the TDWG camera-trap data exchange standard: a Frictionless data package with metadata plus deployments, media and observations tables. It can be published directly to GBIF, with 25 datasets and nearly a million occurrences in the WildAlbum portal. She explained how easy extensibility threatens interoperability and why the classificationMethod/classifiedBy fields no longer capture modern AI pipelines. She then summarised evaluations by the Safe and Sound bioacoustics project and the COST action Insect AI, plus feedback from Trapper users. Together they call for device-neutral hardware fields, recording schedules, audio media fields, an assertions table, all classifications rather than only consensus, and a models table. Work continues through the NLBIF-funded Safer and Sounder project and on GitHub.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Camtrap DP fits data from any stationary sensor, and converging community feedback shows how to extend it for AI provenance and multimodal monitoring.
content_items.why_it_matters: Passive sensors are producing huge multimodal datasets processed by AI. Standardising how AI detections and model provenance are recorded keeps these data comparable and FAIR across camera traps, audio and insect monitoring.

content_items.title: FAIR² Drones: An AI-Ready Standard for Cross-Domain Wildlife Drone Dataset

programme.title: FAIR² Drones: An AI-Ready Standard for Cross-Domain Wildlife Drone Dataset
programme.session: SYM25B From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract: Animal ecology data collection using drones requires a substantial investment of time, expertise, and financial resources. Yet most existing datasets serve only a single research community, limiting interdisciplinary reuse. We propose a unified drone dataset standard, FAIR² Drones, that bridges ecology, robotics, and computer vision by building on existing FAIR and AI-ready data frameworks while adding essential platform metadata and annotation specifications. Our standard enables datasets to simultaneously support ecological analysis, robotics algorithm development, and computer vision model training and benchmarking. We provide open-source validation tools, reference implementations, and multimodal extensions linking drone imagery with complementary sensors, such as camera traps, GPS, and acoustics. By standardizing metadata across disciplines, this framework maximizes the scientific return on investment for costly field deployments and accelerates cross-domain collaboration in environmental monitoring.

content_items.title: Causal Mosaic Schema: Encoding Causal Claims in Ecological Literature as Machine-Actionable Knowledge Graphs

programme.title: Causal Mosaic Schema: Encoding Causal Claims in Ecological Literature as Machine-Actionable Knowledge Graphs
programme.session: SYM25B From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Ecological evidence synthesis increasingly relies on large language models to extract knowledge. Yet most extraction pipelines discard the very information that makes causal claims scientifically defensible: what type of evidence supports the claim, how strong is it, and what kind of causal relationship is established. Without a schema that encodes these properties, extracted claims are superficially machine-readable but epistemically opaque.

Causal Mosaic is a LinkML schema that addresses this gap. It merges the Ecolink Model (ELM) entity structure with an annotation framework based on Illari and Russo’s "causal mosaic" approach. We represent causation as a relation between state changes. Each causal node decomposes into an entity, a measurable attribute, and a direction of change. Each edge carries four annotation layers: claim strength, philosophical account of causation (mechanistic, interventionist, probabilistic, and others), fifteen features that further characterize the causal relationship, and an evidential basis grounded in the view that mechanistic and probabilistic evidence is jointly required to establish causation.

The schema produces a single canonical labeled property graph renderable as natural language (cf. Rosetta Statements), Fuzzy Cognitive Maps, Evidence Gap Maps, and RAG retrieval indices. Edges are grounded in source text spans and carry full provenance, supporting round-tripping from graph back to literature.

We present the schema design, an LLM-assisted extraction pipeline validated against author-reviewed annotations, and a construct validity study for a DFG-funded expert elicitation workshop. Causal Mosaic enables biodiversity knowledge graphs that represent not just what causes what, but how we know it and how confident we should be.

actual.identification_notes: Speaker name rendered 'Tim Almen' by ASR; the chair earlier referred to a 'causal Bayesian schemas' talk. Co-author names are garbled (e.g. 'Lars Voet' = Lars Vogt). The questioner is unnamed.

content_items.summary: Tim Alamenciak opened with the Bandon Marsh restoration in Oregon, where re-flooding produced a salt marsh mosquito outbreak because restoration and mosquito ecology knowledge were siloed. He then presented the Causal Mosaic Schema, a LinkML labelled property graph schema based on Illari and Russo's mosaic view of causality. Nodes describe changes in ontology-grounded entities and attributes. Edges carry four annotation layers (claim strength and linguistic expression, philosophical account, 16 causal features, evidential basis) plus provenance, and annotation needs LLM assistance to scale. The resulting graph can feed evidence gap maps, fuzzy cognitive maps, Bayesian belief network structures and priors, and RAG for practitioners. He also set out its limits: no effect sizes, a Western-science and peer-reviewed-literature focus, and reliance on LLM annotation.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Encoding how and how strongly the literature claims causation, not just what causes what, can link siloed ecological knowledge into decision-support tools for practitioners.
content_items.why_it_matters: Restoration and conservation decisions depend on causal knowledge scattered across disciplines. A schema that preserves evidential strength and provenance makes LLM-assisted synthesis more defensible.
key_points: Bandon Marsh: plugging drainage ditches restored tidal flooding but created standing water and a salt marsh mosquito outbreak, closing a golf course and prompting a public health advisory.
Restoration ecology and mosquito ecology knowledge exist in silos and are not interoperable; EcoWeaver aims to connect them for practitioners.
Causal Mosaic is a LinkML labelled property graph schema inspired by Illari and Russo's 'Causality', developed with Chris Mungall's group at Lawrence Berkeley National Lab.
Nodes represent changes: entity type (taxon, environmental variable, management process, environmental process), ontology-grounded entity term, state/change qualifier, measured attribute and scope.
Edges: 11 causal predicates, ~67 fields, 16 causal features and 8 philosophical accounts in 3 families, organised in four layers. Claims are transcribed as authors made them, not evaluated.
The mosquito example alone gives 14 articles and 238 nodes; a graduate student manually annotated two papers in two months, so LLM-assisted annotation is necessary.
Outputs: evidence gap maps, fuzzy cognitive maps (Kosko), Bayesian belief networks (structure and prior ranges, not fully automatic) and RAG over the graph.

content_items.title: LifeGate: Extending a Global Visual PhyloMap into a Structured Biodiversity Knowledge System

programme.title: LifeGate: Extending a Global Visual PhyloMap into a Structured Biodiversity Knowledge System
programme.session: SYM25B From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
LifeGate (https://lifegate.idiv.de/) is a biodiversity information platform centered on the “PhyloMap”, a visual representation of biodiversity that enables exploration of taxa across multiple hierarchical levels of the Tree of Life. Unlike conventional biodiversity portals based mainly on text search, the PhyloMap provides a navigable overview of phylogenetic relationships from kingdoms to species. The platform integrates taxonomy, images, phylogenetic information, and links to biodiversity literature.

A new project aims to transform LifeGate into a structured and interoperable biodiversity knowledge system by converting descriptive taxonomic knowledge into machine-interpretable biodiversity data. We combine ontology-based modeling, biodiversity knowledge graphs, and AI-assisted information extraction workflows. Domain-specific templates and OWL ontologies are being developed to represent morphological, ecological, and taxonomic characteristics and to support semantic integration with infrastructures such as GBIF.

The workflow integrates expert curation with semi-automated extraction from taxonomic literature using natural language processing and large language models. Extracted entities and relationships are validated through ontology constraints before integration into the LifeGate knowledge graph. A major long-term objective is the development of structured, visually supported identification and faceted search workflows derived from taxonomic descriptions and trait information.

This contribution presents the existing PhyloMap and its extension toward structured biodiversity knowledge integrating visualization, semantic interoperability, and AI-assisted curation.

It also plans to turn LifeGate from a standalone application into a connected part of the knowledge ecosystem through APIs, shared ontologies and knowledge graphs, and integration with Catalogue of Life and ChecklistBank.

programme.title: Discussion
programme.session: SYM25B From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data

actual.identification_notes: Scheduled 15-minute discussion (event-266), held as a standing panel of both sessions' speakers after the last talk. A short warm-up discussion led by an organizer addressed as 'Dave' took place at 06:55:39-06:59:50 while waiting for the next speaker, and is included as a second source segment. Several panellists are unnamed in the transcript; attributions are inferred from content and are marked as such. The GBIF speaker is addressed as 'Joe' (ASR, uncertain). content_items.summary: The SYM25 speakers took questions on AI-ready biodiversity data, moderated by Hilmar Lapp. Panellists agreed that AI-readiness depends on purpose, like fitness for use. That is why FAIR4AI is distinguished from task-specific AI-readiness, though aggregation mixes purposes and shared benchmark snapshots remain valuable. On benefits to data providers, Tanya Berger-Wolf described dataset-side 'recipes' for agents, identifiers propagating from the smallest data unit through aggregations, and a CyVerse/NEON pilot where models register their use against operationalised permissions. Asked what is hardest now, panellists named reluctance to open data to tech-giant harvesting, pushback in Latin America and Africa over data sovereignty and digital sequence information, and data heterogeneity as the root of AI bias. A GBIF voice countered with strong demand for open data in the BID programme and Indigenous data work. A final question on ontologies drew views on ontology governance, explainability and knowledge graphs as the part of LLM systems that users can control.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: AI-readiness is purpose-dependent, and the hardest remaining problems are social: trust, attribution, governance and data sovereignty, where ontologies and knowledge graphs offer some control and explainability.
content_items.why_it_matters: The panel brought together the symposium's threads and set out open problems (value flowing back to data providers, sovereignty, heterogeneity, ontology governance) that infrastructures and standards bodies such as TDWG and GBIF will need to address.
key_points: Warm-up: an audience member asked how to persuade data providers that their contributions will still be acknowledged when their data are used by AI agents, noting they had not seen a strong solution.
AI-readiness depends on purpose: data are purpose-driven models of the world, and like data quality it is fitness for use, hence the FAIR4AI vs AI-ready distinction.
Devil's advocate: aggregated datasets mix purposes, so each researcher must define fitness for their use; shared cleaned benchmark snapshots are still important.

Bidirectionality: add 'recipes'/skills to datasets for agents; propagate identifiers from the smallest data unit through every aggregation so citations and value flow back; store data once and reference derivatives.
The CyVerse pilot with NEON operationalises data use and licensing permissions per model and use case, with models registering use so attribution and valuation propagate back.

Hardest challenges: people withholding data from tech-giant harvesting; open data framed as Western/colonial ('doctrine of digital discovery'); the DSI debate at CBD COP16 moving toward biodiversity digital information; >90% of biodiversity data from private, Indigenous and local community land.

Counterpoint from GBIF: the BID call drew over 1,000 applications requesting €48 million, less than 5% fundable, all requiring open data. Indigenous communities are willing to share when done properly.
Data heterogeneity (protocols, image resolution, compression) drives AI bias.

Ontologies: they give a backbone of certainty but have a governance problem needing inclusive, transparent processes. They can partly de-black-box LLMs, and knowledge graphs and ontologies are the parts of LLM systems that users can control.

How do data providers benefit from AI use of their data?
What is hardest now that AI makes some things easier?
What is the role of ontologies in AI?

We cannot control what LLMs were trained on, but we can control the ontologies and knowledge graphs used with them.

content_items.title: How Literature Services can Support & Benefit from Biodiversity Publication and Data Standards?

programme.title: How Literature Services can Support & Benefit from Biodiversity Publication and Data Standards ?
programme.session: CO5 Digital Tools for Data Discovery, Resolution and Exchange
programme.abstract:
Rapid growth of biodiversity literature makes it difficult to retrieve precise, relevant, and interoperable knowledge. Traditional bibliographic catalogues mainly rely on metadata and abstracts, limiting fine-grained discovery and large-scale reuse.

This presentation explores how literature services can support biodiversity publication and data standards. Using BiodiversityPMC, developed within the SIB Literature Services (SIBiLS), we demonstrate how structured, machine-readable publications enable advanced indexing, semantic enrichment and concept-based retrieval across heterogeneous sources.

The SIBiLS platform integrates taxonomic treatments from Plazi, biodiversity-related documents from Zenodo and full-text articles from biodiversity journals (e.g., EJT, Pensoft). By leveraging structured formats, persistent identifiers and domain ontologies, it transforms publications into AI-ready contents that can be cross-linked and queried at scale. We will also demonstrate how pre-computed literature selection through Triage supports Biodiversa+ communities.

Through simple examples, attendees will perform advanced searches via the web interface, explore semantic annotations and test selected API calls for programmatic access, including MCP calls from AI bots.

content_items.title: From NetCDF to Web Maps: Building an Open-Source Web GIS for Biodiversity Data Cubes

programme.title: From NetCDF to Web Maps: Building an Open-Source Web GIS for Biodiversity Data Cubes
programme.session: CO5 Digital Tools for Data Discovery, Resolution and Exchange
programme.abstract:
Essential Biodiversity Variables (EBVs) provide a standardized framework for monitoring global biodiversity change and supporting international biodiversity assessments. However, there is still a lack of accessible web-based infrastructures that allow multidimensional biodiversity datasets to be explored consistently across spatial and temporal scales. This limits the usability of biodiversity information for research, policy support, and decision-making.

In this presentation, we introduce the EBV Visualizer, a lightweight open-source Web GIS for the interactive exploration of biodiversity data cubes. The application complements the EBV Data Portal by enabling users to visualize and analyze multidimensional raster datasets directly in the browser. The visualizer is built entirely with open-source technologies using vanilla JavaScript, Leaflet.js for interactive web mapping, and Chart.js for temporal analytics and visualization. The backend infrastructure relies on THREDDS Data Server and ncWMS to serve NetCDF datasets efficiently through dynamic tile rendering and caching of multidimensional raster data.

The platform enables users to explore biodiversity variables across space, time, and thematic dimensions, while supporting interactive analyses such as temporal trends for countries, protected areas, or other regions of interest. By combining OGC data standards (netCDF, WMS) with lightweight web technologies, the EBV Visualizer lowers technical barriers to biodiversity data access and contributes to open, interoperable, and FAIR biodiversity infrastructures.

speakers.name: Christian Langer
speakers.affiliation: iDiv (German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research)

actual.identification_notes: The speaker said he had changed the title slightly but covered the same topic (the EBV Data Portal visualiser). ASR renders GEO BON as 'GeoBon', ncWMS as 'NCWMS/NC WMS', THREDDS as 'SWATS' once, and COG as 'Currant' (uncertain). Questioner self-identified as Guillaume Body, French Biodiversity Agency.

content_items.summary: Christian Langer presented the EBV Data Portal (portal.geobon.org) and its visualiser for Essential Biodiversity Variable data cubes. EBVs are modelled datasets that sit between raw observations and indicators, and the EBV Cube format stores them as NetCDF with metadata and four dimensions (x, y, time, entity). The portal offers a metadata catalogue, API, DOIs and versioning. The lightweight vanilla-JavaScript web GIS talks to a THREDDS server through ncWMS for map tiles (e.g. gorilla habitat suitability in 1990) and time series for trends in any user-defined region, with DAP4 chunked access. The cons are server limits for very high-resolution global layers (downscaled ×10 for display), THREDDS not being cloud-native (Zarr would be needed) and ncWMS not being a strict OGC WMS.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: A simple open-source stack of NetCDF, THREDDS/ncWMS and vanilla JavaScript makes multidimensional biodiversity data cubes browsable and analysable in the browser.
content_items.why_it_matters: EBVs are meant to link raw biodiversity data to policy indicators. Making their data cubes easy to explore spatially and over time lowers barriers for researchers and decision-makers.
key_points: EBVs (GEO BON) are measurements describing biodiversity across time, space and entity: eight classes, e.g. species populations with species distribution as a variable.
EBVs act as middleware between raw data (in situ, remote sensing, GBIF occurrences) and indicators (aggregated trends).
The EBV Cube format is NetCDF with metadata and four dimensions (x, y, time, entity) and covers species, traits, habitats, genetics, phenology and more. It is not a competitor to Darwin Core.
The EBV Data Portal provides a searchable metadata catalogue, API, automatic DOIs and version control.

programme.title: Local scientific name resolution using custom data sources
programme.session: CO5 Digital Tools for Data Discovery, Resolution and Exchange
programme.abstract:
Scientific name verification is crucial for biodiversity informatics workflows, enabling researchers to reconcile name-strings against authoritative taxonomic databases, detect misspellings, resolve synonyms, and retrieve accepted names and vernacular names. GNverifier is a tool that provides this capability with high quality and a throughput exceeding 2,000 name-strings per second. For several years, it has operated exclusively as a centralized web service.

Here, we present GNverifier as an easily installed local application that supports custom datasets, including private ones, not available in the centralized service. Data can be seamlessly converted from Darwin Core Archives, CSV, TSV, pipe-delimited files, Catalogue of Life Data Packages, and plain scientific name-string text files.

This functionality is driven by two new applications: sf and gndb. The sf tool converts the aforementioned data formats into an intermediate Species File Group Archive (SFGA) format, which gndb then imports into the GNverifier database. While standard GNverifier datasets are downloaded automatically by gndb, custom and private datasets are imported directly from the local file system. Once the database is built, the local GNverifier instance exposes the same REST API and web interface as the centralized service, but provides the specific datasets required for a given research project. This enables workflows that demand strict data sovereignty or reproducibility.

GNdb is open-source under the MIT license at https://github.com/gnames/gndb. Pre-built binaries for Linux, macOS, and Windows are available on the releases page, and the tool can also be installed via 'go install' or compiled from source.

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded video played after the moderator could not find the scheduled 4:30 talk's recording. Speaker name rendered 'Dima Mazarin' and GNverifier as 'Gen vérifier' by ASR; SFGA/sfwork rendered 'SF WORK'. No Q&A.

content_items.summary: Dmitry Mozzherin presented GNverifier, a scientific name reconciliation tool with fuzzy, partial and authorship matching, over 80 million pre-indexed records from more than 100 datasets, and throughput above 2,000 names per second. It can now run locally as well as at verifier.globalnames.org. Local use suits proprietary, institutional or specialised datasets, offline fieldwork, frequent updates and faster, slimmer databases. The new GNdb tool, part of the Species File Group's SFWork approach, ingests Species File Group Archive (SFGA) files. SFGA can be used directly without database conversion, and the sf and harvester programs produce it from Darwin Core archives, ColDP, CSV/TSV or plain name lists. This replaces error-prone ad-hoc parsing and ingests Catalogue of Life in minutes rather than hours.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: GNverifier can now be run locally over any custom or private name datasets, using the standardised SFGA format and GNdb, with the same API as the central service.
content_items.why_it_matters: Local, reproducible name verification against private or project-specific checklists supports data sovereignty and field use, a need that centralised services cannot meet.
key_points: GNverifier does partial, fuzzy and authorship matching over >80 million records from >100 datasets at >2,000 names per second.
It runs locally or via the central service at verifier.globalnames.org with the same workflow.
Reasons for local use: datasets missing from the central service (proprietary, institutional, specialised), offline/field use, updating datasets at will, and including only needed datasets for speed.
Previous ingestion of diverse, non-standard formats was painful (encoding, malformed metadata XML, delimiter and field-count errors).
GNdb, part of SFWork, ingests SFGA (Species File Group Archive) files, which are usable immediately without conversion into a database.

Pipeline: sf / harvester convert DwC-A, ColDP, CSV/TSV and text to SFGA → gndb populate into Postgres (custom datasets need YAML metadata and IDs ≥1000) → gndb optimize (denormalised view) → gnames service → gnverifier web/CLI/API.
Catalogue of Life can now be ingested in minutes instead of hours.

notable_claims.claim: GNverifier has pre-indexed more than 80 million records across more than 100 biodiversity datasets.
GNverifier can process more than 2,000 names per second.
With GNdb, Catalogue of Life can be ingested in minutes instead of hours.

future_work: Support more dataset formats and streamline the pipeline based on user feedback.
